CALIFORNIA AGE-APPROPRIATE DESIGN CODE ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · https://www.acme.com

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, Civil Code § 1798.99.28 et seq. (added in 2022 by AB 2273) — a state statute directed at businesses whose online services, products, or features are likely to be accessed by children under 18, requiring, among other things, a Data Protection Impact Assessment, default privacy settings favoring a high level of privacy, an age estimation practice, and restrictions on certain uses of a child's personal information. It also describes the ongoing federal court litigation, NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta, which has enjoined enforcement of some of the Act's provisions on First Amendment and vagueness grounds while leaving others in effect, as those facts may relate to Acme, Inc.'s online service, product, or feature located at https://www.acme.com. This information sheet does not itself determine whether Acme, Inc.'s online service, product, or feature is “likely to be accessed by children” within the meaning of the Act, does not constitute a Data Protection Impact Assessment or a privacy notice, and does not tell Acme, Inc. what to do about any specific product, design feature, or practice.

COVERAGE TRIGGER: THE STATUTE'S OWN “LIKELY TO BE ACCESSED BY CHILDREN” TEST
The Age-Appropriate Design Code Act does not apply to every online service, product, or feature that a child could theoretically visit. Civil Code § 1798.99.30(b)(4) defines “likely to be accessed by children” to mean that, based on six separately enumerated indicators, it is reasonable to expect that the online service, product, or feature would be accessed by children: whether it is directed to children under the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act; whether it is determined, based on competent and reliable evidence regarding audience composition, to be routinely accessed by a significant number of children; whether it carries advertisements marketed to children; whether it is substantially similar to a service, product, or feature routinely accessed by a significant number of children; whether it has design elements known to be of interest to children, such as games, cartoons, music, or celebrities who appeal to children; and whether a significant amount of its audience is determined, based on internal company research, to be children. Separately, § 1798.99.30(b)(1) defines “child” or “children,” unless otherwise specified in the title, to mean a consumer or consumers who are under 18 years of age.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Likely to be accessed by children” means it is reasonable to expect, based on the following indicators, that the online service, product, or feature would be accessed by children:(A) The online service, product, or feature is directed to children as defined by the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (15 U.S.C. Sec. 6501 et seq.).(B) The online service, product, or feature is determined, based on competent and reliable evidence regarding audience composition, to be routinely accessed by a significant number of children.(C) An online service, product, or feature with advertisements marketed to children.(D) An online service, product, or feature that is substantially similar or the same as an online service, product, or feature subject to subparagraph (B).(E) An online service, product, or feature that has design elements that are known to be of interest to children, including, but not limited to, games, cartoons, music, and celebrities who appeal to children.(F) A significant amount of the audience of the online service, product, or feature is determined, based on internal company research, to be children."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.99.30(b)(4) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, definition of “likely to be accessed by children” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.99.30.)
  "“Child” or “children,” unless otherwise specified, means a consumer or consumers who are under 18 years of age."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.99.30(b)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, definition of “child” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.99.30.)
  Known gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.99.30 — subdivision (b)(4) (the six-indicator coverage test) and subdivision (b)(1) (the definition of “child”) — they are not independent of one another. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business. The statute's own text does not state that all six indicators must be present, or that any particular combination is required; a Ninth Circuit panel has since read the provision, on the record before it, as meaning that satisfying any single indicator is sufficient, a case-law gloss addressed in a companion clause of this document rather than restated here. This clause does not quote § 1798.99.30(a), which separately incorporates the California Consumer Privacy Act's definitions (including its definition of covered “business” and that definition's revenue and volume thresholds) except where the Act specifies otherwise; a reader wanting the verified text of that CCPA “business” threshold should consult this corpus's existing CCPA documents, which quote it directly. This clause does not determine whether any specific online service, product, or feature in fact satisfies any of the six indicators, which is a fact-specific evidentiary question this document does not resolve. As of the most recent Ninth Circuit ruling reviewed for this document, no injunction is currently in effect against enforcement of this coverage definition itself; that litigation history is addressed in a companion clause.

CORE AFFIRMATIVE DUTIES AS CODIFIED: DATA PROTECTION IMPACT ASSESSMENT, AGE ESTIMATION, AND DEFAULT PRIVACY SETTINGS
As codified, Civil Code § 1798.99.31(a) requires a business that provides an online service, product, or feature likely to be accessed by children to take several affirmative actions. Before offering a new online service, product, or feature to the public, the business must complete a Data Protection Impact Assessment for any online service, product, or feature likely to be accessed by children and maintain documentation of that assessment for as long as it is likely to be accessed by children, biennially reviewing all such assessments. The business must estimate the age of child users with a reasonable level of certainty appropriate to the risks that arise from its data management practices, or, as an alternative the statute itself provides, apply the privacy and data protections afforded to children to all consumers instead of estimating age. The business must also configure all default privacy settings provided to children to settings that offer a high level of privacy, unless it can demonstrate a compelling reason that a different setting is in the best interests of children.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Before any new online services, products, or features are offered to the public, complete a Data Protection Impact Assessment for any online service, product, or feature likely to be accessed by children and maintain documentation of this assessment as long as the online service, product, or feature is likely to be accessed by children."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.99.31(a)(1)(A) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.99.31.)
  "Estimate the age of child users with a reasonable level of certainty appropriate to the risks that arise from the data management practices of the business or apply the privacy and data protections afforded to children to all consumers."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.99.31(a)(5) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, age estimation requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.99.31.)
  "Configure all default privacy settings provided to children by the online service, product, or feature to settings that offer a high level of privacy, unless the business can demonstrate a compelling reason that a different setting is in the best interests of children."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.99.31(a)(6) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, default privacy settings requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.99.31.)
  Known gap: This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.99.31(a) — paragraph (1)(A) (the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement), paragraph (5) (age estimation), and paragraph (6) (default privacy settings) — they are not independent of one another. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business. This clause quotes only the opening sentence of the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement in paragraph (1)(A); it does not separately quote the detailed list of factors that paragraph (1)(B) requires such an assessment to address (including whether a product's design, algorithms, or targeted advertising could harm children, and whether it collects sensitive personal information of children) — that list of factors is the specific statutory text a Ninth Circuit panel held likely facially violates the First Amendment, addressed in a companion clause of this document rather than restated here. As of the most recent Ninth Circuit rulings reviewed for this document, the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement described in this clause is currently under a preliminary injunction and is not being enforced, while the age estimation requirement described in this clause is not currently enjoined; the default privacy settings duty described in this clause was not separately addressed in the Ninth Circuit rulings reviewed for this document, and this document does not represent that it has or has not been the subject of any injunction. That litigation history is addressed in companion clauses. This clause does not determine what specific default settings, age-estimation method, or assessment content would satisfy the statute for any specific business's specific service.

PROHIBITED ACTIONS AS CODIFIED: DATA USE RESTRICTIONS AND THE DARK PATTERNS RESTRICTION
Civil Code § 1798.99.31(b) also lists actions a business that provides an online service, product, or feature likely to be accessed by children shall not take. Among them, the business shall not use the personal information of any child in a way that the business knows, or has reason to know, is materially detrimental to the physical health, mental health, or well-being of a child; the statute lists several related restrictions on profiling children by default, collecting or retaining personal information beyond what is necessary, and using personal information for purposes other than those for which it was collected, each subject to exceptions the business bears the burden of demonstrating. Separately, the statute prohibits a business from using dark patterns to lead or encourage children to provide personal information beyond what is reasonably expected to provide the online service, product, or feature, to forego privacy protections, or to take any action the business knows, or has reason to know, is materially detrimental to the child's physical health, mental health, or well-being.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Use the personal information of any child in a way that the business knows, or has reason to know, is materially detrimental to the physical health, mental health, or well-being of a child."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.99.31(b)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, restriction on materially detrimental use of a child's personal information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.99.31.)
  "Use dark patterns to lead or encourage children to provide personal information beyond what is reasonably expected to provide that online service, product, or feature to forego privacy protections, or to take any action that the business knows, or has reason to know, is materially detrimental to the child’s physical health, mental health, or well-being."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.99.31(b)(7) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, dark patterns restriction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.99.31.)
  Known gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.99.31(b) — paragraph (1) (the general materially-detrimental-use restriction, quoted in full) and paragraph (7) (the dark patterns restriction, quoted in full) — they are not independent of one another. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business. This clause paraphrases, rather than quotes, paragraphs (2) through (4) (profiling, collection/retention, and purpose-limitation restrictions) and does not quote paragraphs (5), (6), or (8) (precise geolocation restrictions and the age-estimation-data-retention limit) at all; a reader wanting those provisions' exact text should consult the statute directly. As of the most recent Ninth Circuit ruling reviewed for this document, a panel affirmed a preliminary injunction against enforcement of both provisions quoted in this clause — paragraphs (1) through (4) and paragraph (7) — on the ground that their reliance on the undefined terms “material detriment,” “best interests,” and “well-being” renders them unconstitutionally vague, a due process holding independent of the First Amendment content-based-speech theory addressed in a companion clause; that litigation history, including the currently enjoined status of these specific provisions, is addressed in a companion clause rather than restated here. This clause does not determine whether any specific use of a specific child's personal information would in fact be materially detrimental, which the litigation history noted above indicates is itself a live, contested legal question.

ENFORCEMENT: EXCLUSIVE ATTORNEY GENERAL AUTHORITY, CIVIL PENALTIES, AND NO PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION
The statute states its own enforcement mechanism and confirms who may bring an action under it. Civil Code § 1798.99.35(a) provides that a business that violates the title is subject to an injunction and liable for a civil penalty of not more than $2,500 per affected child for each negligent violation, or not more than $7,500 per affected child for each intentional violation, assessed and recovered only in a civil action brought in the name of the People of the State of California by the Attorney General. Separately, § 1798.99.35(d) states that nothing in the title serves as the basis for a private right of action under the title or any other law — the statute's own text confirms there is no private right of action for a consumer to sue directly under it. The statute also included a notice-and-cure mechanism: if a business is in substantial compliance with the Data Protection Impact Assessment provisions, the Attorney General must give written notice before initiating an action, and the business avoids civil penalty for any violation it cures within 90 days of that notice and confirms in writing to the Attorney General.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any business that violates this title shall be subject to an injunction and liable for a civil penalty of not more than two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500) per affected child for each negligent violation or not more than seven thousand five hundred dollars ($7,500) per affected child for each intentional violation, which shall be assessed and recovered only in a civil action brought in the name of the people of the State of California by the Attorney General."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.99.35(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, civil penalties and exclusive Attorney General enforcement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.99.35.)
  "Nothing in this title shall be interpreted to serve as the basis for a private right of action under this title or any other law."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.99.35(d) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, no private right of action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.99.35.)
  "If, within 90 days of the notice required by this subdivision, the business cures any noticed violation and provides the Attorney General a written statement that the alleged violations have been cured, and sufficient measures have been taken to prevent future violations, the business shall not be liable for a civil penalty for any violation cured pursuant to this subdivision."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.99.35(c)(2) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, 90-day notice-and-cure mechanism (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.99.35.)
  Known gap: This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.99.35 — subdivisions (a) (penalties and Attorney General-only enforcement), (d) (no private right of action), and (c)(2) (the notice-and-cure mechanism) — they are not independent of one another. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business. As of the most recent Ninth Circuit rulings reviewed for this document, the notice-and-cure provision quoted in this clause, § 1798.99.35(c)(2), is currently under a preliminary injunction and is not being enforced, while the general Attorney General-exclusivity, penalty, and no-private-right-of-action provisions quoted alongside it have not themselves been enjoined in the litigation this document reviewed; that litigation history, including why the notice-and-cure provision was enjoined, is addressed in a companion clause rather than restated here. This clause does not address whether some other statute, such as California's Unfair Competition Law, might supply a separate enforcement avenue; that question was not researched for this clause. This clause also does not quote § 1798.99.35(b) (deposit of recovered penalties into the Consumer Privacy Fund) or § 1798.99.35(e) (the Attorney General's regulatory authority), which were reviewed as part of the same fetched section but are not separately detailed here.

NETCHOICE V. BONTA: THE DATA PROTECTION IMPACT ASSESSMENT REQUIREMENT AND THE NOTICE-AND-CURE PROVISION ARE ENJOINED
The Age-Appropriate Design Code Act has been under continuous federal court challenge since before it took effect. In 2022, NetChoice, LLC, a trade association of online businesses, sued California's Attorney General in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, arguing the Act violates the First Amendment; the district court preliminarily enjoined the Act in its entirety in 2023. On the State's appeal, the Ninth Circuit, in NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta (“NetChoice I”), 113 F.4th 1101 (9th Cir. 2024), vacated most of that injunction and remanded for further proceedings, but affirmed it as to one specific provision: the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement. The panel held that NetChoice was likely to succeed in showing that provision facially violates the First Amendment because the statutory factors such an assessment must address — including whether a product's design, algorithms, or content could harm children — require a business to consider content or proxies for content, triggering First Amendment review. The panel also affirmed the district court's holding that the Act's notice-and-cure provision was not grammatically severable from the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement, so it too remained enjoined. A subsequent Ninth Circuit panel, ruling on a later appeal in the same case, confirmed that this specific holding continues to control, stating that the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement “remains enjoined and is not at issue in this appeal.”

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The panel held that NetChoice was likely to succeed in showing that the CAADCA’s requirement that covered businesses opine on and mitigate the risk that children may be exposed to harmful or potentially harmful materials online facially violates the First Amendment. The panel therefore affirmed the district court’s decision to enjoin the enforcement of that requirement, and the other provisions that were not grammatically severable from it."
  — NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta (“NetChoice I”), 113 F.4th 1101 (9th Cir. 2024), Ninth Circuit, official case summary: DPIA requirement facially violates the First Amendment (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10042522/netchoice-llc-v-bonta/)
  "That requirement remains enjoined and is not at issue in this appeal."
  — NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta, No. 25-2366 (9th Cir. Mar. 12, 2026), Ninth Circuit, confirming the DPIA injunction remains in effect and describing NetChoice I's severability holding (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10807860/netchoice-llc-v-bonta/)
  Known gap: Both citations in this clause concern the same underlying litigation, NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta — the first is to the Ninth Circuit's 2024 opinion itself (NetChoice I), and the second is to a later Ninth Circuit opinion in the same case that quotes and confirms NetChoice I's holding; they are sequential rulings in one ongoing case rather than fully independent corroborating sources, though each is drawn from a separately published, official Ninth Circuit opinion fetched directly for this clause. This document could not independently re-fetch and read the full text of the 2024 NetChoice I opinion beyond its official case summary (itself fetched directly) because of a research-session rate limit on the legal database used; the quoted language describing NetChoice I's DPIA and notice-and-cure holdings is drawn from that official case summary and from the later panel's own direct quotation of NetChoice I in its 2026 opinion, both fetched and read in full for this clause, rather than from an independent read of NetChoice I's full opinion text. This is a preliminary injunction, not a final judgment: the underlying case remains pending in the district court, and this clause states the litigation's posture as of the most recent, most complete decision this document's research located, not a final resolution. This clause does not restate the statutory text of the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement or the notice-and-cure provision, which are quoted in companion clauses of this document; it also does not address the current status of the coverage definition, age estimation requirement, or data use and dark patterns restrictions, addressed in a companion clause.

CURRENT STATUS: COVERAGE DEFINITION AND AGE ESTIMATION NOT ENJOINED; DATA USE AND DARK PATTERNS RESTRICTIONS REMAIN ENJOINED FOR VAGUENESS; CASE STILL PENDING
On remand from NetChoice I, NetChoice sought, and the district court granted, a second preliminary injunction against the entire Act on a new theory: that the coverage definition itself is content based and triggers strict scrutiny for the whole statute. The State appealed again. In a March 12, 2026 opinion, a Ninth Circuit panel (the same panel that decided NetChoice I) rejected that theory and vacated the injunction as to the coverage definition, holding that NetChoice had not carried its burden, on the record developed below, to show that a substantial number of the coverage definition's applications are unconstitutional. The panel likewise vacated the injunction as to the age estimation requirement, holding it could not determine on that record whether the requirement facially violates the First Amendment. However, the panel affirmed the injunction as to the data use restrictions and the dark patterns restriction — not on First Amendment grounds, but because their reliance on the undefined terms “material detriment,” “best interests,” and “well-being” renders them unconstitutionally vague under the Due Process Clause. Finally, the panel vacated the district court's ruling that the Act's remaining valid provisions are not severable from the still-enjoined notice-and-cure provision, holding the record did not yet permit that determination, and remanded the entire case to the district court for further proceedings. As of this document's most recent check, the litigation remains in a preliminary injunction posture with no final judgment on the merits, and the district court proceedings on remand had not yet been located or reviewed for this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The panel held that NetChoice is not likely to succeed on the merits of its facial challenge to the CAADCA’s coverage definition, which consists of six separately enumerated indicators enabling online businesses to determine whether they are subject to the CAADCA."
  — NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta, No. 25-2366 (9th Cir. Mar. 12, 2026), Ninth Circuit, vacating the injunction against the coverage definition for failure to carry the facial-challenge burden (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10807860/netchoice-llc-v-bonta/)
  "We therefore affirm the district court’s injunction with respect to the data use and dark patterns restrictions on vagueness grounds."
  — NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta, No. 25-2366 (9th Cir. Mar. 12, 2026), Ninth Circuit, affirming the injunction against the data use and dark patterns restrictions on vagueness grounds (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10807860/netchoice-llc-v-bonta/)
  Known gap: Both citations in this clause are drawn from the same March 12, 2026 Ninth Circuit opinion (different passages of that one document), not independent corroborating sources, though each passage was independently located and verified as an exact quotation of the fetched opinion text. This is one specific, dated appellate ruling in a case that the opinion itself remands for further district court proceedings; it is not a final judgment, and the enforceability picture it describes could change again as the case continues. This clause does not resolve the current injunction status of the Act's separate “policy enforcement requirement,” Civil Code § 1798.99.31(a)(9), which the district court had enjoined but which the March 2026 opinion's own footnote states was “not at issue in this appeal” — a genuine, disclosed gap in this document's research rather than an implied statement that the provision is or is not currently enforceable. This clause also does not independently restate the statutory text of the coverage definition, the age estimation requirement, or the data use and dark patterns restrictions, each quoted in companion clauses of this document, or the First Amendment holding regarding the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement, addressed in a companion clause.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate that Jordan Lee, on behalf of Acme, Inc., has received and reviewed this information sheet describing California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act and the current status of NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta.

Prepared by: Jordan Lee
On behalf of: Acme, Inc.
Date: September 4, 2026

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 1798.99.31(b) also lists actions a business that provides an online service, product, or feature likely to be accessed by children shall not take. Among them, the business shall not use the personal information of any child in a way that the business knows, or has reason to know, is materially detrimental to the physical health, mental health, or well-being of a child; the statute lists several related restrictions on profiling children by default, collecting or retaining personal information beyond what is necessary, and using personal information for purposes other than those for which it was collected, each subject to exceptions the business bears the burden of demonstrating. Separately, the statute prohibits a business from using dark patterns to lead or encourage children to provide personal information beyond what is reasonably expected to provide the online service, product, or feature, to forego privacy protections, or to take any action the business knows, or has reason to know, is materially detrimental to the child's physical health, mental health, or well-being.

expectedJSON.body: The statute states its own enforcement mechanism and confirms who may bring an action under it. Civil Code § 1798.99.35(a) provides that a business that violates the title is subject to an injunction and liable for a civil penalty of not more than $2,500 per affected child for each negligent violation, or not more than $7,500 per affected child for each intentional violation, assessed and recovered only in a civil action brought in the name of the People of the State of California by the Attorney General. Separately, § 1798.99.35(d) states that nothing in the title serves as the basis for a private right of action under the title or any other law — the statute's own text confirms there is no private right of action for a consumer to sue directly under it. The statute also included a notice-and-cure mechanism: if a business is in substantial compliance with the Data Protection Impact Assessment provisions, the Attorney General must give written notice before initiating an action, and the business avoids civil penalty for any violation it cures within 90 days of that notice and confirms in writing to the Attorney General.

expectedJSON.body: The Age-Appropriate Design Code Act has been under continuous federal court challenge since before it took effect. In 2022, NetChoice, LLC, a trade association of online businesses, sued California's Attorney General in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, arguing the Act violates the First Amendment; the district court preliminarily enjoined the Act in its entirety in 2023. On the State's appeal, the Ninth Circuit, in NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta (“NetChoice I”), 113 F.4th 1101 (9th Cir. 2024), vacated most of that injunction and remanded for further proceedings, but affirmed it as to one specific provision: the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement. The panel held that NetChoice was likely to succeed in showing that provision facially violates the First Amendment because the statutory factors such an assessment must address — including whether a product's design, algorithms, or content could harm children — require a business to consider content or proxies for content, triggering First Amendment review. The panel also affirmed the district court's holding that the Act's notice-and-cure provision was not grammatically severable from the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement, so it too remained enjoined. A subsequent Ninth Circuit panel, ruling on a later appeal in the same case, confirmed that this specific holding continues to control, stating that the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement “remains enjoined and is not at issue in this appeal.”

citations.quote: The panel held that NetChoice was likely to succeed in showing that the CAADCA’s requirement that covered businesses opine on and mitigate the risk that children may be exposed to harmful or potentially harmful materials online facially violates the First Amendment. The panel therefore affirmed the district court’s decision to enjoin the enforcement of that requirement, and the other provisions that were not grammatically severable from it.

expectedJSON.body: On remand from NetChoice I, NetChoice sought, and the district court granted, a second preliminary injunction against the entire Act on a new theory: that the coverage definition itself is content based and triggers strict scrutiny for the whole statute. The State appealed again. In a March 12, 2026 opinion, a Ninth Circuit panel (the same panel that decided NetChoice I) rejected that theory and vacated the injunction as to the coverage definition, holding that NetChoice had not carried its burden, on the record developed below, to show that a substantial number of the coverage definition's applications are unconstitutional. The panel likewise vacated the injunction as to the age estimation requirement, holding it could not determine on that record whether the requirement facially violates the First Amendment. However, the panel affirmed the injunction as to the data use restrictions and the dark patterns restriction — not on First Amendment grounds, but because their reliance on the undefined terms “material detriment,” “best interests,” and “well-being” renders them unconstitutionally vague under the Due Process Clause. Finally, the panel vacated the district court's ruling that the Act's remaining valid provisions are not severable from the still-enjoined notice-and-cure provision, holding the record did not yet permit that determination, and remanded the entire case to the district court for further proceedings. As of this document's most recent check, the litigation remains in a preliminary injunction posture with no final judgment on the merits, and the district court proceedings on remand had not yet been located or reviewed for this document.
